content.title: Version Control Solves the Memory Problem
content.hook: Imagine you are working on a page.
content.context:
At 10:00, it works.

At 10:30, you make three changes.

At 11:00, something is broken.

You stare at the code and think:

> “It worked before. What did I change?”

That question is the problem version control is designed to make easier.

**Git records a history of changes so you can see what changed, when it changed, and which version you want to work from.**

It is not a magical undo button. It is a system for recording and comparing versions of a project.
goals: Understand what version control is for and why engineers keep a history of deliberate changes instead of relying on copied folders or memory.

content.question: Which situation is easiest to recover from?

options.text: You have one folder containing the current files and no history.
You have the current files plus a sequence of deliberate saved versions you can compare.
You have five copies of the folder named `final`, `final2`, `final-real`, `final-new`, and `final-new-2`.
You remember that the broken behavior appeared “sometime this morning.”

feedback.correct: Version control gives you a structured history. Random copies preserve files, but they do not give you a reliable model of what changed between versions.
feedback.incorrect: Version control gives you a structured history. Random copies preserve files, but they do not give you a reliable model of what changed between versions.

content.title: The core idea
content.text:
For this module, keep one sentence in your head:

**Git helps you answer: “What changed, what version do I have, and how do I safely move my work to another version?”**

That single idea will explain most of the commands you learn next.

content.title: A better mental model
content.text:
Think of your project history like a row of deliberate snapshots:

```text
A ---- B ---- C ---- D
      ^           ^
   working    current good
   version    version
```

Each saved point represents a known state of the project.

You can inspect the differences between states.

You can create a new line of work without destroying the old one.

You can share your history with teammates.

activities.title: Which sentence is the most useful?

content.question:
A teammate says, “Git is just a place to upload code.”

Which response is more accurate?

options.text: Yes. Uploading is the entire point.
Git records project history and supports safe changes; sharing with teammates is one part of that workflow.

feedback.correct: Sharing matters, but the deeper value is the history and control over changes.
feedback.incorrect: Sharing matters, but the deeper value is the history and control over changes.
